facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus lived in Australia during the early Late Cretaceous, approximately 94 million years ago.
facts.quote: Diamantinasaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod from Australia that lived during the early Late Cretaceous, about 94 million years ago.

facts.statement: The species D. matildae was first described and named in 2009 by Scott Hocknull and colleagues from fossils found in the Winton Formation.
facts.quote: The type species of the genus is D. matildae, first described and named in 2009 by Scott Hocknull and colleagues based on fossil finds in the Winton Formation.

facts.statement: Specimens AODF 0603 and AODF 0604 were described in 2009 by Scott Hocknull and colleagues.
facts.quote: The two dinosaurs found, known from specimens catalogued as AODF 0603 and 0604 were described in 2009 by Scott Hocknull and his colleagues.

facts.statement: The genus name combines the Diamantina River with the Greek word for lizard, and the species name references the song "Waltzing Matilda".
facts.quote: The species name is a reference to the song "Waltzing Matilda", written by Banjo Paterson in Winton, while the generic name is derived from the Diamantina River, running nearby the type locality combined with the Greek sauros, meaning "lizard".

facts.statement: The Diamantinasaurus discovery was the largest dinosaur find in Australia since Muttaburrasaurus in 1981.
facts.quote: The find was apparently the largest dinosaur discovery in Australia that was documented since that of Muttaburrasaurus in 1981.

facts.statement: By 2025, six additional specimens had been described and nicknamed Alex, Oliver, Ann, Devil Dave, Ian, and Judy.
facts.quote: As of 2025, additional specimens have been described since its initial description, with each specimen being nicknamed as the following: "Alex" for AODF 0836, "Oliver" for AODF 0663, "Ann" for AODF 0906, "Devil Dave" for AODF 0666, "Ian" for AODF 0844 and "Judy" for AODF 0888.

facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus was a medium-sized titanosaurian measuring 16 meters long and weighing up to 25 tonnes.
facts.quote: Diamantinasaurus was a medium-sized titanosaurian, measuring 16 m long and weighing up to 25 t.

facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus was a large quadrupedal herbivore.
facts.quote: Like other sauropods, Diamantinasaurus would have been a large quadrupedal herbivore.

facts.statement: A 2023 study described specimen AODF 0906, which preserved a more complete skull estimated at 50 cm in length.
facts.quote: In 2023, Poropat and colleagues described a new specimen AODF 0906, which preserved the more complete skull with an estimated total length of approximately 50 cm.

facts.statement: The skull shape of Diamantinasaurus was more similar to brachiosaurids than to derived titanosaurs, suggesting a close relationship with the Argentinian titanosaur Sarmientosaurus.
facts.quote: The skull was overall more similar in shape to that of brachiosaurids than derived titanosaurs, and it had similar features to those on the known cranial material of the Argentinian titanosaur Sarmientosaurus which confirmed their previously assumed close phylogenetic relationship.

facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus possessed at least five, and possibly six, sacral vertebrae.
facts.quote: Diamantinasaurus possessed at least five, possibly six, sacral vertebrae.

facts.statement: The known fossil material of Diamantinasaurus includes almost the entire right forelimb, plus the left humerus and left first metacarpal.
facts.quote: Almost all the right forelimb is known from Diamantinasaurus, although the left humerus is known in addition to the right, and the left first metacarpal is known while the right is unpreserved.

facts.statement: A diagnostic feature of Diamantinasaurus is that the glenoid articulation of the scapula is rotated outward, a trait unique among somphospondylans.
facts.quote: Diagnostic of Diamantinasaurus, the glenoid (humerus) articulation of the scapula is rotated to the outside, differing from all other somphospondylans.

facts.statement: The scapula of Diamantinasaurus is robust with a round cross-section, distinguishing it from other somphospondylans.
facts.quote: The scapula of Diamantinasaurus is robust, having a more round cross-section than other somphospondylans.

facts.statement: The humerus of Diamantinasaurus is 1.068 meters long and has a prominently curved proximal surface similar to Opisthocoelicaudia and Saltasaurus.
facts.quote: The proximal surface of the 1.068 m humerus is prominently curved as in the derived titanosaurs Opisthocoelicaudia and Saltasaurus.

facts.statement: The ulna of Diamantinasaurus measures 70 cm in length, while the radius measures 67.5 cm.
facts.quote: The ulna is 70 cm long, while the radius is 67.5 cm.

facts.statement: In the hand of Diamantinasaurus, the middle metacarpal (41.2 cm) is longer than the next longest metacarpal (37.5 cm).
facts.quote: the middle metacarpal being the longest (41.2 cm Mc III compared to next longest 37.5 cm Mc II)

facts.statement: The manus of Diamantinasaurus possesses a thumb claw and a phalangeal formula of 2–1–1–1–1.
facts.quote: the presence of a thumb claw; and the presence of multiple phalanges, having the phalangeal formula 2–1–1–1–1.

facts.statement: Preserved hindlimb elements of Diamantinasaurus include the left ilium, both pubes, both ischia, and the entire right leg excluding the foot, though some are fragmented.
facts.quote: The left ilium, left and right pubes, left and right ischia, and entire right leg lacking the foot are preserved for Diamantinasaurus, although some bones are highly fragmented and poorly preserved.

facts.statement: The top edge of the Diamantinasaurus ilium is broken, exposing small internal chambers similar to those found in Alamosaurus, Epachthosaurus, Lirainosaurus, Saltasaurus, and Sonidosaurus.
facts.quote: The top edge of the ilium is broken, revealing numerous small internal camerae, as present in the titanosaurs Alamosaurus, Epachthosaurus, Lirainosaurus, Saltasaurus and Sonidosaurus.

facts.statement: In Diamantinasaurus, the ischium is 68% the length of the pubis and expands medially to close the entire pelvic floor.
facts.quote: The entire ischium is only 68% of the length of the pubis as in other titanosaurs, and also expands medially so the entire floor of the pelvis is closed.

facts.statement: The fibula of Diamantinasaurus is 76.9 cm long and is of intermediate robustness, bordering on being gracile.
facts.quote: The fibula is 76.9 cm long, and is intermediately robust, although close to gracile.

facts.statement: A process on the posterior side of the astragalus is unique to Diamantinasaurus among all sauropods, serving as an autapomorphy.
facts.quote: A process on the posterior side of the astragalar body is unique among all sauropods, making it an autapomorphy of Diamantinasaurus.

facts.statement: Poropat et al. (2014) hypothesized that the absence of carpal bones in Diamantinasaurus fossils indicates their genuine absence in life, similar to Opisthocoelicaudia and Alamosaurus.
facts.quote: Because of the completeness of the forelimb material, the absence of carpal bones among the preserved material was presumed by Poropat et al. (2014) to be related to their genuine absence in life, as in Opisthocoelicaudia and Alamosaurus.

facts.statement: Poropat et al. (2014) suggested based on Diamantinasaurus that all titanosaurs possessed ossified phalanges, a view that contrasts with earlier studies.
facts.quote: The presence of large numbers of phalanges in Diamantinasaurus was used by Poropat et al. (2014) to suggest that all titanosaurs actually had ossified phalanges contrasting earlier studies.

facts.statement: A 2014 study placed Diamantinasaurus as a lithostrotian in a relatively derived position within Titanosauria.
facts.quote: In a 2014 study, it was found that the genus was placed as a lithostrotian in both large phylogenies, in a relatively derived position in Titanosauria.

facts.statement: Gorscak & O'Connor (2019) recovered Diamantinasaurus as a saltasaurid using parsimony analysis, but a variable-rates Bayesian analysis placed it just outside Saltasauridae.
facts.quote: Gorscak & O'Connor (2019) in their description of Mnyamawamtuka recovered Diamantinasaurus as a saltasaurid using a parsimony phylogenetic analysis, while a variable-rates Bayesian phylogenetic analysis recovered it as falling just outside Saltasauridae.

facts.statement: The genus Diamantinasaurus was described by Hocknull et al.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Hocknull et al.

facts.statement: The species Diamantinasaurus matildae was described by Hocknull et al. in 2009.
facts.quote: species_authority: Hocknull et al., 2009

facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus lived in the middle Cretaceous, approximately 98 to 95 million years ago (Turonian stage), in what is now Australia.
facts.quote: que vivió a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 98 a 95 millones de años, en el Turoniense, en lo que es hoy Australia.

facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus fossils were recovered from the Winton Formation, dated to approximately 93 million years ago.
facts.quote: It was recovered from the fossil-rich section of the Winton Formation, which can be dated to approximately 93 million years ago.

facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus was relatively small for a titanosaur, possibly reaching 15 to 16 meters in length and 15 to 20 tons in weight.
facts.quote: Diamantinasaurus era relativamente pequeño para un ser un titanosauriano, posiblemente alcanzando entre 15 y 16 metros de longitud y 15 a 20 toneladas de peso.

facts.statement: Fossilized gut contents revealed that Diamantinasaurus engaged in bulk feeding and multi-level browsing, consuming conifers, seed ferns, and flowering plants.
facts.quote: The specimen provided direct dietary evidence of bulk feeding and multi-level browsing, resulting in consumption of conifers, seed ferns and flowering plants.

facts.statement: The completeness of plant material in the gut suggests sauropods like Diamantinasaurus used their mouths minimally and relied on fermentation and gut microflora for digestion.
facts.quote: The relative completeness of the plant material also indicated that sauropods used their mouths minimally to process their food and relied on "fermentation and their gut microflora for digestion".

facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus bones are distinguished from other sauropods by their overall robusticity and multiple specific features.
facts.quote: Diamantinasaurus bones can be distinguished from other sauropods because of the overall robusticity as well as multiple specific features.

facts.statement: A 2011 study described the smallest positively identified titanosaur embryo, which shares the most features with Diamantinasaurus and Rapetosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2011, the smallest positively identified titanosaur embryo was described. Although it was uncovered in Mongolia, the embryo shares the most features with Diamantinasaurus and Rapetosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2025, fossilized gut contents from the subadult specimen AODF 0888 were described in detail.
facts.quote: In 2025, the fossilized gut contents from a referred subadult specimen AODF 0888 was described in detail.

facts.statement: The species Diamantinasaurus matildae was described in 2009 by Scott Hocknull and colleagues in the online journal PLoS ONE.
facts.quote: La especie tipo es D. matildae, que fuera descrita en el periódico en línea PLoS ONE por el paleontólogo del Museo de Queensland Scott Hocknull y sus colaboradores en 2009.

facts.statement: The holotype of Diamantinasaurus was discovered during four seasons of excavations near Winton, Queensland, Australia.
facts.quote: El holotipo de Diamantinasaurus se descubrió por primera vez durante cuatro temporadas de excavaciones cerca de Winton, Queensland, Australia.

facts.statement: The species name references the song "Waltzing Matilda" written in Winton, while the genus name combines the Diamantina River with the Greek word for lizard.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie es una referencia a la canción "Waltzing Matilda", escrita por Banjo Paterson en Winton, mientras que el nombre genérico se deriva del Río Diamantina, corriendo cerca de la localidad donde fuera encontrado, combinada con el vocablo sauros del griego, que significa "lagarto".

facts.statement: The discovery of Diamantinasaurus ended a pause in Australian sauropod discoveries, being the first named sauropod in over 75 years.
facts.quote: El descubrimiento de Diamantinasaurus puso fin a una pausa en el descubrimiento de nuevos dinosaurios de su grupo en Australia, con el primer saurópodo nombrado en más de 75 años.

facts.statement: An additional sample, AODF 836, was described in 2016 and includes parts of the skull such as a nearly complete cranial box and a left squamosal.
facts.quote: En 2016 se describió una muestra adicional, AODF 836 . Incluye partes del cráneo, que incluyen una escamoso izquierdo, una caja craneal casi completa , un surangular derecho y varios fragmentos.

facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus is considered a more derived sauropod than Wintonotitan wattsi, belonging to the Lithostrotia clade within Titanosauria.
facts.quote: Comparado con el contemporáneo Wintonotitan wattsi este sauropódo es más derivado, dentro del clado Lithostrotia en Titanosauria.

facts.statement: A 2014 study placed the genus in Lithostrotia in a relatively derived position within Titanosauria based on two major phylogenetic analyses.
facts.quote: En un estudio de 2014, encontró el género como litostrotiano en ambos grandes análisis filogenético, en una posición relativamente derivada en Titanosauria.

facts.statement: A 2016 phylogenetic analysis found Diamantinasaurus as a non-lithostrotian titanosaurian and the sister taxon to the contemporary Savannasaurus.
facts.quote: Otro análisis filogenético realzado en 2016, lo encontró como un titanosauriano no litostrótico y el taxón hermano del contemporáneo Savannasaurus.

facts.statement: The fossils were found in the middle-upper section of the Winton Formation, dating to the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Esta localidad se encuentra en la sección media superior de la Formación Winton, que data del Cenomaniense en el Cretácico Superior.

facts.statement: The time range for Diamantinasaurus is estimated from 100.5 to 89.8 million years ago, spanning the Cenomanian to Turonian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Turonian (100.5 to 89.8 million years ago)

facts.statement: The dinosaur was found in a clay layer between sandstone layers, interpreted as a deposit from an abandoned river channel.
facts.quote: Diamantinasaurus se encontró en una capa de arcilla entre las capas de arenisca , interpretada como un depósito del brazo muerto de un antiguo río.

facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus bones can be distinguished from other sauropods due to their general robusticity and multiple specific characteristics.
facts.quote: Diamantinasaurus los huesos se pueden distinguir de otros saurópodos debido a la robusticidad general, así como a múltiples características específicas.

facts.statement: Australovenator was found at the same site directly associated with Diamantinasaurus, along with bivalves, fish, turtles, crocodiles, and various plants.
facts.quote: También se encontró en el sitio a Australovenator, asociado directamente con Diamantinasaurus, bivalvos, peces, tortugas, cocodrilos y varias plantas.

facts.statement: The parent group for the genus Diamantinasaurus is Diamantinasauria.
facts.quote: Parent group: Diamantinasauria

facts.statement: Diamantinasaurus is classified within the class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia
